title: Twice as fast. But only ten milliseconds saved?

scenes.heading: A faster FFT. A faster system?
captions: Suppose a Fourier computation becomes twice as fast.
Does the whole system become twice as fast? Pause and predict.

scenes.heading: First, measure the whole journey.
captions: Imagine sequential work taking one hundred milliseconds.
Fourier computation takes twenty. Everything else takes eighty.

scenes.heading: Only the Fourier block shrinks.
captions: Halve the Fourier time: twenty milliseconds becomes ten.
The other eighty milliseconds stays unchanged.
Ten plus eighty is ninety. We saved ten milliseconds.

scenes.heading: Kernel speed is not system speed.
captions: Overall speedup is old time divided by new time.
One hundred over ninety is about one point one one, not two.

scenes.heading: Even an instant FFT has a ceiling.
captions: Even zero Fourier time leaves eighty milliseconds.
In this model, the speedup limit is one point two five.

scenes.heading: Four questions. Four different tests.
captions: Arithmetic complexity asks how operation counts grow.
Numerical stability asks how computation errors behave.
Latency measures elapsed time for the whole workload.
Readiness needs validation against system deadlines.

scenes.heading: Faster is useful. Readiness is more.
captions: Check accuracy, data movement, and worst-case deadlines.
This toy arithmetic proves no new FFT or real-time grid capability.

scenes.heading: Measure the bottleneck. Then improve it.
captions: Explore the fraction improved and its speedup in our Marimo lesson.
Fourier methods connect algorithms to latency—not automatically to readiness.
